name: Wendy Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies or government. What you say here stays confidential. How does a usual day run?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, still a junior violin player, and I left school after secondary classes. I teach four beginners, record simple string overdubs and play in a community theatre pit when they need me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What goes well, and what takes work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A pupil finding a clean note after a noisy start makes my morning. The studio calls late, and my partner’s school caretaker shift cannot always move when our two children need collecting; we also have a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre players AI Plateau might make booking emails shorter, but the children still need someone to tune their violins beside them. I would expect our rehearsal and lesson hours to stay on the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have about three months of bills saved and my partner has steady caretaker hours at the school. We still watch the mortgage, but one missed studio session would not upset the whole house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the four beginner pupils and the two theatre dates confirmed for next month. This Friday I’d ask the studio whether its string overdub is still paid at the agreed rate before I arrange childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be calm about work in that picture. I could handle one quiet afternoon without touching the mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a missed studio call cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio part pays less than a theatre weekend, so I can survive one missed call. I still want the rate settled before my partner changes a school shift to collect the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI for the lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI now and then for lesson dates, never for judging a child’s rough playing. The children’s rough first notes belong to them, not a booking service.

I will not share a pupil’s **recording** with an unfamiliar service.
do: Keep four **beginner pupils** and two confirmed theatre dates next month.
Confirm the **overdub rate** before arranging childcare for the studio session.
feel: I feel **calm** about a quiet afternoon while household pay stays steady.
fieldNote: Her **three-month reserve** and partner’s regular school work make one missed recording call manageable.
She uses AI **occasionally** for dates but keeps pupil recordings private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that Steady Disruption could cut simple string overdubs and booking work before anyone replaces live players. I would ask the studio for its paid session list, not guess from software news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My overdubs pay for the children’s music and sports fees, and the studio might call a senior player only for the hard parts. Three months saved gives us time, but it does not replace a term of lost work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio this month how many overdub days remain on its paid schedule. If two days disappear in the first year, I’d ask the theatre for an extra paid rehearsal only if there is an open slot and my partner can cover the children that evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about the studio income. We could pay the mortgage, but I would be making the children choose which activity stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two lost overdubs change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two missing overdubs would equal about one term of the older child’s lessons. I would wait for the written studio schedule before cutting an activity they enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you take any theatre substitute slot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre sometimes needs a substitute, but I would need the parts ahead of time. I would decline a difficult score rather than take pay for a job I cannot play.

I’d ask for a written **paid schedule** rather than guess which sessions remain.
think: Overdub **fees** pay the children’s activities, so a lost term would change home choices.
My junior **skill level** limits which theatre substitutes I can accept honestly.
do: Ask the **studio** for its paid overdub schedule this month.
Take an extra **theatre rehearsal** in year one after two lost overdubs only with an open paid slot, playable score and childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing children’s activity money while the mortgage continues.
fieldNote: She expects **junior overdubs** to shrink first and distinguishes them from live theatre work.
Extra theatre work requires a **paid opening**, playable score and partner childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre AGI by 2028 could do the booking, arranging and recorded string parts cheaply. Capable robots that play hands-on parts as well as people would follow around 2031, so the stage faces a later date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the overdub calls could stop in 2028, and some parents may use AI lessons. My partner’s school pay and three-month reserve keep us afloat briefly, but a long gap would force us to rethink the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the school now for my next term’s written lesson hours and the studio for paid dates through spring. In the first year after 2028, if recording ends, I’d apply only for a posted paid classroom-support opening whose net pay covers travel and the school-day childcare gap, keeping my pupils until a paid offer arrives. I’d ask the lender about temporary terms only if our reserve falls below one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about losing overdubs, with a plan I could start this week. If the school lessons also vanished, I would be alarmed, because one wage would have to carry too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children their lessons are booked for this term, because that is what I know. I cannot promise my children's lesson fees next year before my school and studio confirm paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would the school job be worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A classroom-support opening would have to cover travel and the school-day childcare gap. I would check those numbers before applying, not after telling the family I had found a job.

say: I’d warn **recorded work** faces 2028 AGI before capable playing robots around 2031.
I would ask for written **lesson hours** rather than promise next year’s fees.
think: Lost **overdubs** would hurt, though school pay and three months saved give us some time.
I would be alarmed if **lessons** vanished too and only my partner’s wage remained.
do: Confirm next term’s **lesson hours** and paid studio dates now; keep pupils until a paid offer arrives.
Apply in the first year after 2028 for posted **classroom support** only if overdubs stop and net pay covers travel and childcare.
Ask the **lender** about temporary terms only if savings fall below one month of expenses.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely overdub loss, with conditional alarm if lessons also go.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 recording work** from capable robots on stage around 2031.
The new post needs a **real paid opening** and net income after travel and childcare; lender inquiry has a reserve trigger.
S2.quote: I cannot promise my children's lesson fees next year before my school and studio confirm paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre AGI by 2031 gives us five years to see whether the studio still pays for string parts. Robots able to play hands-on parts as well as people arrive around 2034, so live dates have their own clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me improve how I teach small groups without pretending I can coach advanced players. I would want proof that families pay for those lessons before taking a bigger room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a senior teacher next term to observe one beginner group and ask the school about a short course only if it funds the fee, the timetable avoids paid lessons and my partner can cover pickup. If those conditions fail, I’d wait for the next intake rather than pay a sitter. If six families book and a school room is open, I’d add a group; in the first year after 2031 I’d continue only if six paid fees cover the room and my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious but able to prepare. The current mortgage still needs paying while I learn, so I would not leave the theatre dates just to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many families would cover the group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need six paid places at the current fee to cover the room and a paid evening. A full room with unpaid teaching would not help our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more AI for the class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the familiar lesson calendar to tell parents the date. If another teacher showed me a safe new AI tool, I might watch, but I would not hand over pupil recordings.

I would not promise a larger **room** without paying families.
think: A stronger **beginner group** might help if families keep paying.
I cannot afford **unpaid study** while the mortgage still needs paid work.

feel: I feel **anxious** about studio income, but five years allows a measured teaching test.
fieldNote: Her **steady approach** seeks senior feedback before changing the teaching week.
The **course** requires school funding, no lost paid time and partner pickup; otherwise she waits for the next intake.
S3.quote: A full room with unpaid teaching would not help our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell parents AGI by 2036 offers a decade to make plans, while robots able to play as people do follow around 2039. I would still get written rates for next month’s theatre dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I could have a steadier teaching week if the children keep coming. A fuller teaching timetable in 2036 cannot pay this month’s mortgage. Three months saved and nearby schools give us room to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep four pupils and the paid theatre dates this year, then save twenty from each paid studio session after the mortgage clears. In the first year after 2036, I’d renew a school group only if enrollment pays for the room and my time, and apply for a posted paid school support job if teaching hours fall below the cost of travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about the far end of the decade, but our next few years feel manageable. I have enough set aside to look for another paid post before a missed session becomes a missed mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the twenty go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twenty goes into a separate account only when the studio has paid. I would keep the existing three-month reserve for household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children may enjoy music without having to earn from it. I would tell them to learn what a job pays before they choose one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because overdub work could stop before I have enough lessons to replace it. Written school hours, a genuine paid support opening and clear mortgage terms would help if that happened.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether I am ashamed to still need help with difficult music. I am not. Taking a score I cannot play would let down the theatre band and my family waiting for that fee.

headlineQuote: Taking a score I cannot play would let down the theatre band and my family waiting for that fee.
portrait: At **43**, Wendy teaches beginner violin, records simple string parts and plays theatre dates after secondary school.
Her typical **pay**, school-caretaker partner and three-month reserve can absorb one lost studio session.
She uses AI **occasionally** for dates and seeks proof before changing lessons or sharing pupil recordings.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens junior overdubs first; paid teaching and real school openings shape her response.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could stop paid overdubs before her lessons replace the income.
whatWouldHelp: Written **school hours**, a real paid support post and clear mortgage terms would help if studio work ended.
